newsitem.title: USA: US junk funds lure Japan's yield-seeking investors.
newsitem.headline: US junk funds lure Japan's yield-seeking investors.

text.p: Japanese investor cash could provide the next boost of buying power for mutual funds that have already seen record weekly cash inflows this year, according to two U.S. money management companies.

Denver-based INVESCO Asset Management has gone abroad to tempt Japan with clones of two U.S. funds, raising nearly 30 billion yen, or about $242 million, since a roadshow in April, said Fumio Sueshige, deputy president of INVESCO Asset Management Japan Ltd.

Also, Fidelity Investments this month announced its first high-yield specific fund for Japanese investors -- the Fidelity High-Yield Bond Open Investment Trust. Assets under management of the trust were not immediately available.

Typically low returns on local investments will continue to drive private Japanese investors into high-yield trusts, Sueshige said. Exponential growth in these trusts should follow based on the trillions of yen earmarked for overseas bonds or deposits every year, he said.
"Right now when you look at one year investment (in Japan), you get only 0.25 percent or so," Sueshige said. "On the contrary, a high-yield fund is 6.0 or 8.0 percent."
INVESCO has bandied about a figure of $1.0 billion in assets by yearend 1997, according to a manager in Denver.

Even with the recent erosion in the dollar against the yen since May 1, Sueshige maintained that Japanese investors will not shy away from dollar-denominated trusts. The dollar, which hit a four and a half year peak on May 1, on Thursday appeared to find some stability following a steady two-week decline that equated to 10 percent of its value.

"Japanese investors are a little cautious about some forex movement," he said, at the same time insisting the added value of professional management outweighs market jitters. Further, he contends Japanese investors are not threatened by greater volatility of high-yield bonds.

But funds should be reluctant to increase their assets with Japanese investments, said John Bianchi, a managing director and head of Smith, Barney Inc's high-yield funds. Smith, Barney does not offer a high-yield specific fund to the Japanese, although high-yield bonds are present within those that are marketed in Japan.

"It's been our experience that the Japanese tend to be less tolerant of paper losses and high-yield obviously is a market that can produce paper losses depending on where you are in the cycle," Bianchi said.

"Given the volatility characteristics of high-yield it would probably be a mistake to be marketing pure high-yield funds in Japan with spreads as tight as they are," he said, adding that the market was "overheated."
Citing the current heady market sentiment, he had no doubt the funds will be successful in their cash-raising efforts.

INVESCO's high-yield bond fund, or investment trust, an exact clone of the one managed by Jerry Paul in Denver, is distributed through New Japan Securities, Sueshige said. The Income Select Fund, also launched in April, will be distributed through Cosmos Securities.
The Income Select Fund has half of its assets in high-yields and half in U.S. Treasury securities.
The Fidelity fund, which is split between one that offers a currency hedge and one that does not, is distributed in Japan through Nikko Securities Co.
